items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1969-12-04
items.q: My brother Paul played the drums and I had the trumpet. And we visited all the joints of the district. We played with the Negro bands.

ctx.x: My brother Paul played the drums and I had the trumpet. And we visited all the joints of the district. We played with the Negro bands. I could buy them a little shell of beer for a nickel apiece and I was always welcome, John, because they liked the way I played. And it didn't hurt me. I listened to them play, they listened to me. They didn't play my way, but nobody threw us out. And he'd slap that bass and my brother would beat hell out the drums and we'd have a hell of a little bit of a time. And I was welcome.…

items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1973-03-16
items.q: And my brother was my drummer and he was great.

ctx.x: No, I don't know that, Waltz. Yeah.

For the love of might. It was a popular moment. It was one of those things like, I knocked the hell out of Kelly. You know, oh no, no. And I said, for the love of might, and my saxes went into the love of might. And I said to myself, talk about it, quick on the trigger, how did you do it? And my brother was my drummer and he was great. I'd never heard or played with a drummer like him. And he never presumed because of my mother. But I'd be standing in front of that band doing a chorus or something, you know, and…
And all of a sudden the band, I had no background.
